title: Central Africa's Critical Minerals and the Criminal Scramble
summary: Maya and Daniel examine a November 2026 report from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime on Central Africa's critical raw materials. They analyze how global competition for energy transition minerals is opening doors to armed conflict, geocriminality, and elite capture.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome to the podcast. Today we are looking at a major report published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, or GI-TOC. It is titled Vulnerable Wealth: Who Will Profit from Central Africa's Critical Minerals?, written by Zobel Behalal and Romain Esmenjaud.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And this is a study that anyone tracking international security, supply chain resilience, or illicit finance really needs to pay attention to. For years, when people talked about illicit minerals in Central Africa, the conversation was almost entirely about artisanal gold and diamonds. But this report makes a compelling case that critical raw materials—the minerals driving the clean energy transition, digital infrastructure, and advanced defence—are being drawn directly into those very same criminal dynamics.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. The report examines five Central African states: the Democratic Republic of Congo, Gabon, Cameroon, Chad, and the Central African Republic. Sub-Saharan Africa holds roughly thirty percent of the world's critical mineral reserves, and Central Africa sits right at the core of that endowment. Think about copper, lithium, cobalt, coltan, manganese, antimony, and rare earth elements. These are the ingredients for electric vehicle batteries, AI hardware, fighter jets, and guided missiles.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the sheer scale of future demand is staggering. The report notes projections from the International Energy Agency showing that over the next ten to fifteen years, global demand is expected to climb by twenty-eight percent for copper, and by more than three hundred and fifty percent for lithium. That surge has completely flipped the geopolitical script for Central Africa, moving it from what was often treated as a peripheral region right into the center of great power competition.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. Take the DRC, which is by far the regional heavyweight. It produces over seventy percent of the world's cobalt, more than fifty percent of its coltan, and ranks second globally in copper. Mining makes up about ninety-five percent of the DRC's export value and forty percent of its GDP. And it has a lithium deposit in Tanganyika province estimated to be worth at least fifteen billion dollars, with its first certified lithium export occurring in July 2026.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And it is not just the DRC. Gabon is the world's second-largest manganese producer, pulling out close to seven million tonnes in 2024, and it is exploring the Mabounié polymetallic deposit, which reportedly holds the world's second-largest known deposit of niobium, along with rare earths, tantalum, and scandium. Then you have Chad producing antimony in the Tibesti region, Cameroon with battery metals at Nkamouna-Lomié and bauxite at Minim-Martap, and the CAR, which has identified over four hundred and seventy mineral occurrences and brought in a Canadian firm, CVMR Corporation, for satellite exploration.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The opportunity for these states is immense. They can leverage these deposits to renegotiate external partnerships, demand domestic processing, build infrastructure, and create jobs. But the core warning of the GI-TOC report is that this mineral boom is colliding with severe structural vulnerabilities. The authors argue that the question is no longer whether organized crime will penetrate Central Africa's critical minerals sector, but how far it will spread.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's unpack that geopolitical competition first, because the scramble among external powers seems to be actively shaping these vulnerabilities. Historically, China moved first and built a dominant position across the entire value chain—around sixty percent of global rare earth extraction, ninety percent of refining, and eighty to ninety percent of permanent magnet production. In the DRC, Chinese firms heavily dominate copper and cobalt.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right, and now other powers are rushing to catch up. The European Union has signed critical raw materials partnerships with the DRC, Zambia, Namibia, and Rwanda, and is co-financing the Lobito Corridor through its Global Gateway strategy alongside the United States. Gabon confirmed a major deal with France's Eramet in July 2026, which tied manganese concessions to rail modernization on the Trans-Gabon Railway. Meanwhile, the UAE, Japan's JOGMEC, Saudi Arabia, and Indonesia are all striking deals or exploring partnerships across the region.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: The US push detailed in the report is especially striking. Under the Trump administration, there was direct mediation between the DRC and Rwanda leading up to a peace agreement signed at the White House on June 27, 2025. Trump explicitly stated afterward that the US would get, in his words, 'a lot of mineral rights from the Congo.' That was followed in December 2025 by a bilateral strategic partnership granting preferential access for US and aligned entities.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And look at how that translated on the ground in 2026. DRC authorities submitted a priority list of twenty-five mining assets for US partnerships. Astonishingly, that list reportedly included Rubaya, a massive coltan site in North Kivu currently controlled by the armed group M23. And the pressure to clear ground for industrial operators appears to have had immediate social consequences—the report cites sources linking that broader push to the relocation of nearly twenty thousand artisanal miners from the Kamilombe copper and cobalt mine in Lualaba Province in October 2026.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which brings us directly to the first major structural vulnerability: the dynamics between artisanal and small-scale mining, or ASM, and large-scale industrial mining. Why is ASM such a magnet for organized crime?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Because ASM is dispersed, highly informal, involves hundreds of thousands of vulnerable workers, and takes place in remote regions where state oversight is practically nonexistent. While large-scale mining operations produce huge bulk tonnages that are harder to smuggle, ASM is feasible for several high-value critical minerals—like the 3Ts, cobalt, copper, lithium, and nickel. When you have weak regulation and heavy barriers to formalization, artisanal miners become easy prey for armed groups, corrupt officials, and illicit trading networks.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the actors who spent decades running illicit gold and diamond networks are simply pivoting. The report illustrates the existing governance gap with a mind-boggling number from Cameroon: in 2023, Cameroon's government officially declared just twenty-two point three kilograms of gold exports. Yet that same year, the United Arab Emirates recorded imports of more than fifteen tonnes of gold originating from Cameroon.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: A fifteen-tonne gap. That shows you just how porous the borders and institutions are. And we are seeing those exact networks move into critical minerals. Look at the Central African Republic. The report flags Sigma Resources CAR, which secured exploration permits for cobalt, copper, nickel, and lithium. The company is controlled by Sigma Mining, linked to the UAE conglomerate International Holding Co. Back in 2023, Sigma took control of Sigma Gold in the CAR, sourcing gold from the Ndassima concession operated by Russia's Wagner Group. The individual who registered these companies, Saqlain Raza, was named by the UN Group of Experts as involved in smuggling DRC gold to Dubai, though he has denied those claims.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It is a textbook illustration of how murky actors with ties to state-sanctioned mercenaries and illicit trading hubs are positioning themselves right at the ground floor of emerging critical minerals. Now, the report categorizes the primary criminal threats into three distinct risks: armed conflict, geocriminality, and elite capture. Let's start with armed conflict.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The clearest case is eastern DRC. Rubaya produces over fifteen percent of the world's tantalum supply, and it is controlled by the Rwandan-backed rebel group M23. M23 controls the extraction sites, the transit routes, and collection points, levying illegal taxes. According to UN expert reporting cited by GI-TOC, M23 facilitates the transfer of up to about two hundred tonnes of coltan per month into Rwanda, where it is reportedly mixed with domestic production to obscure its illicit origin.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So a mineral that ends up inside western smartphones, rockets, and electronics is actively sustaining an armed rebellion that destabilizes the entire Great Lakes region. And the report warns that the same playbook could unfold in Chad or the CAR, where armed groups have historically survived on gold and diamonds.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. Now, the second risk is what the authors term geocriminality: the use of criminal and hybrid practices by sovereign states to secure strategic advantage. We are seeing major powers target critical mineral supply chains through disinformation and covert influence campaigns.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the report uncovers a fascinating case involving the Lobito Corridor. The corridor is the flagship Western-backed rail line connecting the mining heartlands of the DRC and Zambia to the Angolan Atlantic port of Lobito. In 2023 and 2024, it became the target of a coordinated Russian influence campaign run by Africa Politology—originally Wagner's influence branch, which came under the direct control of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, the SVR, in December 2023.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The authors reviewed a confidential Africa Politology document showing an orchestrated operation across Angola, the DRC, Namibia, and South Africa. They planted fabricated interviews, forged documents, used paid commentators, and stoked local political grievances specifically to inject narratives about Western 'neocolonialism' into Angolan public debate, all to undermine the corridor's viability.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: It mirrors other cases cited in the report, like the Dragonbridge campaign linked to Chinese interests targeting rare earth companies in Australia, Canada, and the US, or bot networks in Myanmar targeting Indian rare earth initiatives. It shows that critical minerals are considered high-value strategic targets for hybrid warfare.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Then we come to the third risk: elite capture. This is where ruling political and military elites abuse state power to monopolize mineral wealth for private enrichment, often hidden behind opaque corporate structures and shell companies. We see this at industrial scales in the DRC, where illegal artisanal copper and cobalt mining on ERG concessions in Lualaba and Haut-Katanga has grown into a quasi-industrial racket worth an estimated two billion dollars a year, operating under the direct protection of security forces and political elites.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the investigation into Chad's antimony sector is perhaps one of the most eye-opening sections of the entire report. Antimony is essential for semiconductors, ammunition, and flame retardants. In Chad, high-grade antimony was discovered in the remote Tibesti region, and within just two years, it was completely captured by a political-security syndicate.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: The report documents how investigative reporting in late 2024 revealed that mining sites in Tibesti were owned by Chadian military generals close to the government. High-purity ore was sold directly to Chinese, Turkish, and Libyan intermediaries, transported across the border to Cameroon, and shipped out through the port of Douala, with profits funneled through offshore accounts in Hong Kong and the UAE.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the Chadian government initially met those revelations with complete silence. It was not until February 2026 that the Ministry of Finance suddenly issued a decree establishing a two percent statistical levy and a twelve point five percent mining tax on antimony exports. Analysts viewed that decree as a quiet official admission that thousands of tonnes had been smuggled out completely unrecorded. In fact, Chadian official statistics showed nearly ten thousand tonnes of raw antimony were exported in 2025, and the finance minister later estimated annual exports would reach nineteen thousand tonnes.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It is an astonishing example of how quickly a newly extracted critical mineral can be fully captured by an entrenched military elite before formal governance frameworks even exist. And what makes all of this worse is that international safeguards appear to be eroding under the pressure for supply security.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is a critical point. While the EU has introduced regulations like the Critical Raw Materials Act and the Batteries Regulation, the overall international regime is fraying. The report highlights moves in the US Congress, supported by the Trump administration, to repeal Section 1502 of the Dodd-Frank Act—the foundational legislation that mandated conflict minerals due diligence for the 3Ts and gold. When consuming nations prioritize speed of access and counter-China geopolitics over governance, due diligence falls by the wayside.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It creates a race to the bottom. So, what does the GI-TOC report recommend to counter these trends? First and foremost, it calls on Central African governments to build comprehensive critical mineral strategies that place organized crime risk mitigation directly at the core of sector governance. This means access to mining licenses and public partnerships must be strictly conditioned on verifiable supply chain traceability and anti-corruption standards.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Second, they urge regional anti-money laundering bodies—specifically GABAC, the Action Group against Money Laundering in Central Africa—alongside the FATF, to update their risk frameworks. Critical mineral supply chains need to be explicitly evaluated for their role in laundering illicit proceeds, financing armed groups, and facilitating capital flight.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Third, the report demands an outright ban on direct or indirect ownership of mining assets by politically exposed persons, or PEPs. Governments must enforce full beneficial ownership transparency and subject mineral traders and intermediaries to strict anti-money laundering requirements. You cannot dismantle elite capture if generals and ministers are allowed to secretly own the concessions.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Fourth, regional governments need to equip their law enforcement, customs, and mining police with actual operational tools—vehicles, communications, forensics—while establishing rigid anti-corruption safeguards within enforcement agencies to stop collusion. They also need cross-border intelligence sharing to target the criminal networks running the trade, not just low-level artisanal diggers or truck drivers.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And finally, a message for mineral-importing countries: adhere to the G7's Évian commitments. Western and Asian powers cannot cut 'security-for-minerals' deals that sacrifice transparency. Trading weapons or political protection for access to copper, cobalt, or tantalum simply legitimizes and protects the very networks driving instability.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: As we wrap up, what are the key takeaways and things to watch in the coming months?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: First, watch whether the US-DRC mineral agreements move forward around contested sites like Rubaya, and what that means for local security and civilian displacement. Second, keep an eye on Chad's antimony sector—whether the new tax decree actually brings transparency, or if the generals' networks continue running ore through Douala illicitly. And third, watch how regional bodies like GABAC respond to illicit financial flows coming out of these critical mineral corridors.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Central Africa's critical minerals have the power to lift millions out of poverty and drive the global transition. But as this report shows, without aggressive enforcement and governance, that wealth will continue to enrich warlords, corrupt elites, and criminal syndicates. The report is Vulnerable Wealth by Zobel Behalal and Romain Esmenjaud, published by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. A fascinating and urgent read.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Thanks for listening, and join us next time as we break down another critical investigation.
